objectives.statement: Multiply a three-digit whole number by one digit using a partitioned area model and a written calculation.
Explain regrouping as preserving place value, including a zero digit in a product or factor.

content.body: A fictional school in Nimba County plans three exercise books for each of 214 pupils. Split 214 pupils into groups of 200, 10 and 4. Each group needs three books per pupil; the three regions together count the whole order.

accessibility.textAlternative: A fictional school in Nimba County plans three exercise books for each of 214 pupils. Split 214 pupils into groups of 200, 10 and 4. Each group needs three books per pupil; the three regions together count the whole order. Connect each region to its full place-value quantities. Find 214 × 3 by splitting it into parts.

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.prompt: Connect each region to its full place-value quantities.

scenes.title: Connect the model to the written calculation

content.body: Multiply each full quantity by three. Twelve ones can be regrouped as one ten and two ones. Regrouping does not create or remove books; it is another way to name the same value.

accessibility.textAlternative: Multiply each full quantity by three. Twelve ones can be regrouped as one ten and two ones. Regrouping does not create or remove books; it is another way to name the same value. Find three exercise books for each of 214 pupils. Step 1: Multiply each place-value quantity. 214 × 3 = (200 × 3) + (10 × 3) + (4 × 3) Step 2: Combine the complete partial products. 600 + 30 + 12 = 642 Step 3: Regroup twelve ones without losing their value. 600 + 40 + 2 = 642

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.problem: Find three exercise books for each of 214 pupils.

steps.text: Regroup twelve ones without losing their value.

scenes.title: Connect the regions to column multiplication

content.body:
Keep hundreds, tens and ones in separate columns. Start at the ones. Four ones times three is twelve ones: write two ones and carry one ten. One ten times three plus the carried ten is four tens. Two hundreds times three is six hundreds. These columns name the same 642 books as the three regions.

| Row | Hundreds | Tens | Ones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carried value | | 1 | |
| Pupils | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| Multiply by | | | 3 |
| Books | 6 | 4 | 2 |

accessibility.textAlternative:
Keep hundreds, tens and ones in separate columns. Start at the ones. Four ones times three is twelve ones: write two ones and carry one ten. One ten times three plus the carried ten is four tens. Two hundreds times three is six hundreds. These columns name the same 642 books as the three regions.

| Row | Hundreds | Tens | Ones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carried value | | 1 | |
| Pupils | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| Multiply by | | | 3 |
| Books | 6 | 4 | 2 | Write 214 times 3 in hundreds, tens and ones columns. Step 1: Align the place-value columns. 214 × 3 Step 2: Ones: keep two ones and carry one ten. 4 × 3 = 12 = 10 + 2 Step 3: Tens: add the carried ten to the three tens. (1 × 3) + 1 = 4 tens Step 4: Hundreds: six hundreds complete the result. 600 + 40 + 2 = 642

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.problem: Write 214 times 3 in hundreds, tens and ones columns.

steps.text: Ones: keep two ones and carry one ten.
Tens: add the carried ten to the three tens.
Hundreds: six hundreds complete the result.

scenes.title: Keep the zero place and the regrouped value

content.body: Try 143 times 3 and 208 times 4. In 208, there are no tens to start with, but multiplying the eight ones can still create tens. A zero digit is not permission to discard value created elsewhere.

prompts.prompt: Show 143 times 3 in columns. Name the value of the carried 1 when twelve tens are regrouped. Use the area partition to check your result.

accessibility.textAlternative: Try 143 times 3 and 208 times 4. In 208, there are no tens to start with, but multiplying the eight ones can still create tens. A zero digit is not permission to discard value created elsewhere. Calculate and interpret the products. 143 times 3: write your answer. 208 times 4: write your answer. Tens formed by 8 times 4 ones: write your answer. Show 143 times 3 in columns. Name the value of the carried 1 when twelve tens are regrouped. Use the area partition to check your result.

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

misconceptions.feedback: The 1 names 100 and the 4 names 40. Their products are 300 and 120, not 3 and 12.
Two hundreds times four is 800; treating the 2 as two ones loses the hundreds.
Eight ones times four makes 32 ones: three tens and two ones, even though the starting tens digit was zero.

hints: Partition the larger factor into full hundreds, tens and ones; retain every regrouped quantity.
afterAttempt: 143 times 3: 429. The 1 names 100 and the 4 names 40. Their products are 300 and 120, not 3 and 12.
208 times 4: 832. Two hundreds times four is 800; treating the 2 as two ones loses the hundreds.
Tens formed by 8 times 4 ones: 3. Eight ones times four makes 32 ones: three tens and two ones, even though the starting tens digit was zero.

content.body: Use column multiplication for 125 times 4. Use a partitioned calculation to check it, then choose either method for 321 times 6. Check that both methods preserve all the place-value quantities, especially when a final digit is zero.

prompts.prompt: Show the column calculation for 125 times 4 and identify each carried quantity. Check it by adding the area-model partial products. Explain why the zero digits in the answer preserve the full value.

accessibility.textAlternative: Use column multiplication for 125 times 4. Use a partitioned calculation to check it, then choose either method for 321 times 6. Check that both methods preserve all the place-value quantities, especially when a final digit is zero. Find each product. 125 times 4: write your answer. 321 times 6: write your answer. Show the column calculation for 125 times 4 and identify each carried quantity. Check it by adding the area-model partial products. Explain why the zero digits in the answer preserve the full value.

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

misconceptions.feedback: The 20 ones formed by 5×4 contribute two tens. Dropping those two tens leaves 480 instead of the complete value.
The 120 from 20×6 includes an additional hundred. Keep it when combining with 300×6 and 1×6.

afterAttempt: 125 times 4: 500. The 20 ones formed by 5×4 contribute two tens. Dropping those two tens leaves 480 instead of the complete value.
321 times 6: 1926. The 120 from 20×6 includes an additional hundred. Keep it when combining with 300×6 and 1×6.

content.body: A pupil writes 125 times 4 as 480 after forming 400, 80 and 20. The partial products were correct, but the last combination lost part of the value. Explain how to repair the combination.

accessibility.textAlternative: A pupil writes 125 times 4 as 480 after forming 400, 80 and 20. The partial products were correct, but the last combination lost part of the value. Explain how to repair the combination. Combine the partial products 400, 80 and 20. A fictional pupil wrote: 400 + 80 + 20 = 480 Which correction preserves every partial product? Options: Ignore 20 because its ones digit is zero.; Combine 80 and 20 as 100, then add it to 400.; Append 20 to 480 to make 48020..

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.question: Which correction preserves every partial product?

options.text: Ignore 20 because its ones digit is zero.
options.feedback: The zero ones digit does not remove the two tens represented by 20.

options.text: Combine 80 and 20 as 100, then add it to 400.
options.feedback: The tens combine to make another hundred, giving a total of 500.
Appending digits changes place values. Add the quantities instead.

scenes.title: Plan a rice delivery in Bong County

content.body: A fictional community rice cooperative in Bong County packs 246 bags with four kilograms of rice in each bag. The team must plan the total mass for delivery. Use a complete calculation and explain one partial product so another pupil can check the plan.

prompts.prompt: Explain what the 40×4 region counts and why all partial products must be kept. For an advanced challenge, show a second valid partition of 246 and prove that the total stays the same.

accessibility.textAlternative: A fictional community rice cooperative in Bong County packs 246 bags with four kilograms of rice in each bag. The team must plan the total mass for delivery. Use a complete calculation and explain one partial product so another pupil can check the plan. What total mass of rice is planned? Kilograms of rice: write your answer. Explain what the 40×4 region counts and why all partial products must be kept. For an advanced challenge, show a second valid partition of 246 and prove that the total stays the same.

offline.fallback: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.prompt: What total mass of rice is planned?

misconceptions.feedback: The forty-bag region is 40×4=160. Treating it as only 40 discards part of the plan.

afterAttempt: Kilograms of rice: 984. The forty-bag region is 40×4=160. Treating it as only 40 discards part of the plan.
